p: Jordan passed her medical exam with no limits.
Marisol put her to work on an oil change with Biscuit's engine open, and quizzed her on carburetor ice, spark plugs and the electrical system.
Reading every line of the maintenance logbooks, Jordan found an emergency beacon battery whose replacement date had passed in March, after Danny died. Marisol replaced it before anyone flew.
On a damp May morning the engine iced up on a long descent and Jordan cleared it with carb heat. Danny's notebook had the same scare, in the same airplane.
Then Marisol showed her a lumpy twist of safety wire from a year of Saturdays Danny spent in her hangar after her divorce, and nobody in the family had known.
Abby Strand. Jordan's instructor. Blunt, quick, and hard to impress.
Walt Herrera. The club's safety officer, and the partner Jordan most needs to win over.
Russ Kim. The fourth partner, who flew Biscuit over the mountains in April.
Marisol Tran. The club's mechanic, who's started letting Jordan in.
Ellie Reyes. Danny and Claire's daughter. She's nine.
Claire Reyes. Danny's widow, Ellie's mother.

Wednesday night Jordan sat at her kitchen table in Aurora with a mug of tea going cold and the Centennial forecast open on her laptop, and for the first ten minutes it looked like a ransom note. Abby had booked her for Thursday at seven, if the weather played nice, on one condition: check the TAF before you text me.

The Centennial forecast, three lines of letters and numbers. The first line starts TAF, KAPA, one three two three two zero Zulu, one four zero zero slash one four two four, then the wind and clouds: three three zero at eight knots, more than six miles, a few clouds at ten thousand. The second line, from oh nine hundred Zulu, has light and variable wind and a clear sky, and the third starts F M one four one five zero zero.

She did what she always did with a call she didn't understand. She took it apart. The FAA's Aviation Weather Handbook was a free PDF, a few hundred pages longer than any protocol binder she'd ever been handed, and she read the section on terminal forecasts twice, the second time with a pen.

TAF, then the airport. Then one three two three two zero Zulu: the forecast was finished on the 13th at 2320 Zulu, which the handbook said was UTC, which a different website said was six hours ahead of Colorado in the summer. Then fourteen hundred slash fourteen twenty four, good from midnight Zulu on the 14th to midnight Zulu at the end of it. They wrote midnight at the end as 24 so nobody would confuse it with the start. She liked that. It was the kind of rule a tired person had written for other tired people.

F M one four one five zero zero meant from 1500 Zulu on the 14th. Nine in the morning, her time. Northwest at ten knots, more than six miles visibility, a few clouds at eight thousand feet. Her lesson was at seven. She'd be back on the ground by eight thirty, before any of it.
She texted Abby a screenshot with her decode typed underneath, line by line, the way she'd hand off a patient. The reply came at 10:06.
A text from Abby Strand. Not bad. Check it again when you wake up. A TAF is a forecast. The weather didn't read it.

Danny's green notebook sat at the other end of the table under her keys. She'd been reading it a few entries at a time, in order, and she'd only skipped ahead once. She set her alarm for 5:55 and went to bed.

At 5:55 the wind outside her bedroom window was pushing the neighbor's recycling bin up the sidewalk one lurch at a time. Jordan sat on the edge of the bed with her phone and pulled the weather before she'd put her feet on the floor.

Centennial, Thursday, 5:53 AM. The METAR: wind three one zero at sixteen knots, gusting twenty seven. Ten miles visibility. A few clouds at eight thousand, scattered at twelve thousand. Temperature twelve, dewpoint minus three, altimeter thirty oh two. After the remarks, A O two, then a peak wind of three one zero at thirty one knots at eleven twenty eight Zulu, and the T group, T zero one one seven one zero two eight. The TAF starts at twelve hundred Zulu with the same sixteen gusting twenty seven. From sixteen hundred Zulu, three two zero at twenty, gusting thirty two, scattered at ten thousand. From oh two hundred Zulu, three three zero at ten, sky clear.

Taped inside her kneeboard was the card Abby had written for her after the carb ice lesson, in blocky marker: STUDENT LIMITS. YOURS UNTIL I SAY. WIND 15. GUSTS NO MORE THAN 10 OVER. CROSSWIND 8. YOU MAKE THE CALL. I'LL TELL YOU IF IT'S WRONG.
It was 6:00. The lesson was at 7.

She types it the way she'd call in a patient. Canceling. METAR 310 at 16 gust 27, peak 31 half an hour ago. TAF has 20 gust 32 from 1600Z, that's 10 local. Over the card on every line. She hits send and sits there in her socks. Ninety seconds, about. Then the phone buzzes against her knee. That's the first smart thing you've done. No emoji, no punctuation to soften it, which from Abby is practically a hug. A second bubble: Briefing room at 8 anyway. Bring coffee. Not the gas station kind.

The current report is already over every limit on the card, and the forecast says it gets worse at 1600Z, which is 10 a.m. here. Cancel early, cancel with the numbers, and I don't have to talk you out of anything. This is what the card is for.

The briefing room window buzzed in its frame whenever a gust came over the ramp, and by 8:15 it was buzzing pretty much full time. Somebody had taped a sign over the light switch that said DO NOT TOUCH THERMOSTAT (RUSS). Abby had copied the morning METAR onto the whiteboard in red marker, all of it, and drawn a fat lopsided box around the end.
Everything after RMK. People skip it. A machine stood out on that field all night measuring this stuff for you, and people skip it. She capped the marker. AO2. And the T group. Go.

AO2 is the automated station that can tell rain from snow. The T group is eleven point seven and minus two point eight. Yep. Zero's plus, one's minus, three digits each, in tenths. Up top it got rounded to 12 and M03. She writes the spread, 14.5, under the box and circles it twice, hard enough that the marker squeaks. Real spread. Remember it. One of these days some kid's going to ask you how high the clouds are and you'll get to be insufferable.

AO2 means automated with a precipitation discriminator. AO1 has no discriminator. The T group is plus 11.7 and minus 2.8 Celsius. The body rounds to whole degrees, so the T group is what you want when the math needs precision.
Walt came in at nine with a box of grocery store donuts, set it on the table, and didn't sit down. Russ says you canceled.

Hm. He picked up a marker, uncapped it, and wrote a METAR on the board from memory in small square capitals, the way a man writes something he's written ten thousand times. Denver, January, some year. I was on shift. Where's the ceiling?

Denver, oh four fifty three Zulu on the fourteenth. Wind zero three zero at eleven, three miles in light snow and mist. Scattered at six hundred, broken at twelve hundred, overcast at three thousand. Minus one and minus two, altimeter thirty oh eight.

Twelve hundred. The broken layer. Walt caps the marker. Twelve hundred above the ground, three miles in snow. I dispatched into that more times than I can count, and I never once sent a Cessna. He takes a donut for himself, which Abby will tell her later is the closest thing to a compliment he has. On his way out he stops at the door. Danny would've gone this morning, you know. He'd have found a reason. He doesn't say whether that's praise or not.
Lowest broken or overcast layer, heights in hundreds of feet above ground level. BKN012 is a 1,200 foot AGL ceiling. The scattered layer under it doesn't count.
After Walt left, Abby turned around the whiteboard, where she'd already written the morning TAF, and underlined FM141600 twice.
Last thing before the boring part. When does this start? On a watch. Not a computer.
The coffee maker gurgled. Out on the ramp a Piper Warrior strained at its tiedowns like a dog that wanted to go for a walk.

Ten. Six hours back in the summer. Abby checks her phone. Which is forty one minutes from now. At 10:04 the window behind her rattles in its frame hard enough that they both look at it, and the windsock across the ramp goes from straight out to straight out and angry. Abby doesn't say anything. She doesn't have to.
Subtract 6 hours in summer, on daylight time, and 7 in winter. 1600Z minus 6 is 1000 local. Every time in a METAR, TAF, AIRMET, SIGMET, PIREP, and winds aloft forecast is Zulu.
Friday night Abby sent homework instead of a time.
A text from Abby Strand. Sat 7am if it's legal and smart. We're climbing to 7,500 over Bennett. Decode the DEN line for me. Why is half of it missing?

Winds and temperatures aloft for Denver, valid twelve hundred Zulu Saturday. The three thousand and six thousand columns are blank. Nine thousand: two six one four, plus oh five. Twelve thousand: two seven two five, minus oh one. Eighteen thousand: two seven four one, minus fourteen. Twenty four thousand: two seven five two, minus twenty six. Thirty thousand: seven six zero two four one.
Jordan worked it out on the back of a pizza flyer. Then she stared at the gaps for a while, the way she'd stare at an empty line on a patient chart.

She texts Abby one line: the low levels are too close to the ground at Denver. Abby texts back: Yes. 3,000 is underground and 6,000 is 570 feet off the ground at DEN. No wind within 1,500 of the station, no temps within 2,500. A minute later: Bonus. Decode 30,000. Jordan subtracts 50 from 76, adds 100 to 02, and sends it: 260 at 102, minus 41. Abby: Show off. See you at 7.

2614+05 is 260 degrees true at 14 knots, plus 5 Celsius. Winds aren't forecast within 1,500 feet of the station's elevation and temperatures aren't forecast within 2,500 feet, and the 3,000 foot level never carries a temperature. 760241 is 260 at 102 knots, minus 41 Celsius.
Twenty five minutes later the club chat lit up.

A message from Russ Kim. taking biscuit to steamboat sunday morning, it's on the calendar, don't me. yes i see the airmets. they're airmets. sigmets are the scary ones. airmets are for gliders and nervous people

Jordan opened the graphical AIRMETs on the aviation weather site. Over the mountains west of Denver on Sunday morning there was a Tango box, moderate turbulence below 18,000, and a Sierra box stuck to the high terrain for mountain obscuration. She'd known Russ for about five weeks, and most of it had been skull emojis.

She types it plainly and adds: The Tango and the Sierra are both over your route Sunday. Not my call, you're the pilot. Just saying what they say. Nothing for four minutes. Then Russ: ok who taught the student to read. Walt: Nobody. She read it. Russ: fine. moving it to next weekend. bringing donuts as penance. marisol do not say anything. Marisol sends a single photo of the whiteboard: ELT BATT, boxed.

Sierra is IFR and mountain obscuration. Tango is moderate turbulence, strong surface wind, and low level wind shear. Zulu is icing and freezing levels. Those are aimed at light airplanes. Saying the facts without the attitude is how a student talks to a pilot with a thousand hours.

Saturday came up clear and dead calm. ATIS: minus one, dewpoint minus three. Biscuit had spent the night tied down on the ramp like always, and in the blue light before sunrise her wings had gone fuzzy. Powdered sugar. On May 16th. Colorado.
Jordan dragged a fingertip down the leading edge and it left a clean wet stripe of maroon paint. You could read the N number on the tail right through the stuff. Abby's text said ten minutes out.

They tow her to the east end of the row, where the sun clears the hangars first, and stand around in it like cows. Forty minutes. Marisol wanders over in a parka with three coffees in a cardboard tray and one of them has JORDAN written on the lid. Danny used to come out with a squeegee and a thermos of hot water. Then he'd stand there yelling at the water for freezing on the windshield. She hands it over. Sun's better. Sun doesn't need a thermos. Wheels up at 7:42, bare dry wings.

The PHAK says an aircraft must be thoroughly cleaned and free of frost before flight. Sun, a heated hangar, or approved deicing all work. Waiting costs a lesson slot. Frost on takeoff can cost the airplane.

Sunday was a cookout at Claire's in Parker. Burgers, on the enormous grill Danny bought the summer he decided he was a grill guy and then used maybe nine times. The patio umbrella was still in its winter cover. His orange Broncos camp chair was still folded up against the back fence with a dried leaf stuck in the hinge. It had been there since March.

Ellie was flat on her back on the trampoline in shin guards and one sock, eating a pickle. Ellie's other sock was on the grass, nowhere near the trampoline. Above her the clouds were coming off the foothills in a herd, big lumpy white ones, and every last one had a bottom so flat you could've set a level on it. Same height, every one. Like a glass shelf.
Aunt Jordan. Why are clouds flat on the bottom?
Somewhere down the block a dog kept barking at nothing. Claire looked over from the grill with the spatula in her hand. She didn't say anything. Danny had been the one for questions like this.

Getting onto a trampoline at thirty five turns out to involve a knee and some swearing under her breath. She lies down next to Ellie anyway. Okay. Driveway gets hot, right? Burns your feet. It heats up the air sitting on it, and hot air goes up. Bubble in a pot of water. But up is colder, so the bubble cools off on the way. And there's water hiding in it. Invisible. Cool it enough and, boom, you can see it. Like your breath in January. Jordan laughs. Like your breath in January. And all the bubbles around here started out about the same, so they all hit cold enough at the same height. That's your shelf. Ellie squints up at it for a while. So the shelf is made of cold. Kind of. You can figure out how high it is with a thermometer. Ellie sits up. Show me. Over at the grill Claire flips a burger she's already flipped, and her shoulders drop about an inch.

Rising air cools at about 3 degrees Celsius per 1,000 feet and its dewpoint drops about half a degree, so they meet at a predictable height. Air with the same surface temperature and dewpoint condenses at the same level, which is why the bases line up flat.

May 28th, a Thursday, and Centennial was showing off. Calm, cool, the windsock hanging like a sleeve. Out west over Evergreen, though, three long gray clouds sat stacked one on another like plates in a cupboard, not moving, edges so smooth they looked cut out with scissors. A guy fueling a Mooney had his phone up taking pictures.

Centennial, Thursday, 6:53 AM. Wind two three zero at four, ten miles, a few clouds at fifteen thousand, nine and minus one, altimeter twenty nine eighty eight. And in the remarks, standing lenticular altocumulus, west through northwest.

The winds aloft over the Divide were 270 at 45 at 12,000. Jordan had looked them up because now she couldn't help it. It was 48 degrees and she was in a fleece she'd regret by ten. Abby was doing the walkaround. Those are pretty. Where do you want to go?

East. The practice area, nowhere near the foothills. Good. Lenticulars. Forty five knots coming over the Divide, and it's sloshing on the far side like a bathtub, and under the sloshing there's rotor. Gorgeous. From Bennett. An hour of smooth air over the wheat. Jordan keeps twisting around in her seat to look at them, which costs her fifty feet on a steep turn and an eyebrow from Abby.

Altocumulus standing lenticular clouds are the classic sign of mountain wave. The METAR even flagged them in the remarks, west through northwest. The turbulence and rotor are on the lee side near the mountains, so the smart plan stays east and keeps distance from the foothills.

The first week of June turned hot. Abby moved the lessons earlier, and still, by 10 a.m. the air over the plains east of the airport was boiling up off the wheat fields. At 7,500 over Bennett, Biscuit hit a bump that lifted Jordan off the seat against her belt, and then another one, and the coffee cup in the side pocket jumped out and rolled under the rudder pedals.
It went on like that for a couple of minutes. Not dangerous. Not fun either. The airspeed needle wandering ten knots each way. Abby's pen bouncing on her kneeboard.
Nobody's reported this. We're on with Denver Approach. Give them a PIREP.

She keys the mic and it comes out almost the way Abby taught her. Denver Approach, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, PIREP. Over Bennett, seven thousand five hundred, Cessna One Seventy Two, moderate turbulence, last two minutes. The controller reads it back and thanks her. Thirty seconds later he passes it to a Bonanza inbound from the east. Abby writes PIREP on her kneeboard and draws a star next to it.

Location, time, altitude MSL, aircraft type, and the hazard with an intensity. That's the required core of a PIREP, plus at least one weather element. Moderate means real changes in altitude or attitude with the airplane under control at all times.

A cold front came down the plains on a Friday night in June, and by Saturday morning the whole city had a lid on it. Jordan woke at 5 to a world the color of dishwater. Her own street ended in gray after about four houses.

Centennial, Saturday, 5:53 AM. The METAR: wind zero seven zero at nine, two miles in mist, overcast at four hundred feet. Temperature nine, dewpoint eight, altimeter thirty twenty one. The TAF has zero seven zero at ten, two miles in mist, overcast at four hundred, and temporarily until fifteen hundred Zulu, half a mile in fog with the overcast down to two hundred. From two thousand Zulu, zero five zero at eight, five miles in mist, broken at twelve hundred. From oh one hundred Zulu, three three zero at six, more than six miles, scattered at five thousand.
The lesson was at nine. Abby hadn't texted. Jordan understood by now that this was on purpose.

She texts Abby: Canceling. East at 9, spread 1, upslope. TAF keeps it upslope all day, northeast at 2000Z, and doesn't turn it northwest till 0100Z, 7 PM. Abby: Agree. Go back to bed. Then: You're getting annoying to teach. Then: Compliment. Jordan gets back under the covers and doesn't sleep. Outside a garbage truck works its way down the block, invisible, beeping.

East wind, a tiny spread, a low overcast after a front: textbook upslope fog. It forms when moist, stable air is pushed up rising terrain and it needs the wind to keep going. It won't burn off like radiation fog while that wind blows.
Saturday the 13th of June was the first true summer day. The TAF had a line Jordan read three times before she left the house.

The Centennial forecast, Saturday, 5:20 AM. Light and variable this morning, a few clouds at twelve thousand. From seventeen hundred Zulu, east at eight, scattered at eight thousand. From two thousand Zulu, one three zero at twelve gusting twenty, scattered at seven thousand, broken at twelve thousand. A thirty percent chance, twenty one hundred to midnight Zulu, of thunderstorms and rain, with cumulonimbus in a broken layer at six thousand. From oh two hundred Zulu, one eight zero at six, scattered at twelve thousand.

Wheels up 10:30. By ten after twelve they were doing power off stalls over the practice area, and each time she rolled out of a clearing turn the stuff to the south had grown. One cloud over the Palmer Divide, twenty five miles off, maybe, had quit being a cloud. It was a tower now. Cauliflower on top, white as a fridge, still going up, and a gray smear hanging under one side of it with ragged strings falling out of the bottom and quitting halfway to the ground.
On an ambulance she'd have called it a scene she didn't like the look of. She knew that feeling. She'd never had it at 7,500 feet.
Abby, who'd seen it ten minutes ago, said nothing at all.

I want to go home. Your airplane. Jordan turns west for home and calls the tower twelve miles out. The ATIS wind is still calm, if you can believe it. They land at 12:41 on 35R. After landing flow, the way Abby taught it: flaps up, carb heat cold, strobes off, mixture leaned for taxi. By 12:55 Biscuit's tied down, gust locks in. At 1:20, from the briefing room window, they watch a wall of brown dust come up the airport from the south and the windsock snap around to point north, and every tied down airplane on the ramp rocks on its ropes at once. Abby checks her watch, then the TAF on her phone. Forty minutes early, she says. Write that down somewhere.

Towering cumulus with virga and a rain shaft means a cell in or near the mature stage. The gust front can arrive well ahead of the rain, and the TAF's timing is a guess. Heading home early, while the home airport is still calm, is the whole plan.

Jordan drove to Parker with the windows down, which was a mistake for about three minutes when the outflow caught her on Parker Road and threw grit across the windshield, and then the air went cool and smelled like wet pavement, and it was the best thing she'd smelled all week.

Claire's kitchen window faced south, over the back fence and the camp chair and the neighbors' roofs, all the way to the long dark rise of the Palmer Divide. The storm was sitting right on top of it. The anvil had spread out across half the sky, flat and white, and under it the base was the color of a bruise, with rain hanging down in sheets you could see move.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Mija the news says hail in Castle Rock. Tell me you are not in that airplane.

She texts back: On the ground since 12:41. At Claire's. Watching it from the kitchen. A pause, the three dots coming and going for a long time. Then: Good. Kiss Ellie. Which was, from her mother, about a paragraph.

Ellie knelt on a kitchen chair with her nose almost on the glass, counting between the flashes and the thunder. Claire stood behind her with a dish towel over her shoulder. Jordan had the green notebook on the counter. She'd brought it on purpose. She'd read ahead last night, finally, and found the page she wanted.

Danny's logbook, a page from June, six years ago. June 17. KAPA to KCOS for lunch, return via KFLY, 2.1. TAF said thunderstorms from 2100. Figured that's nine PM, I'll be home by four, easy. Reader, 2100 Zulu is THREE PM. Found this out at 3 PM over Monument with a black wall in front of me and a Bonanza on frequency asking ATC if anybody knew where the gust front was. Landed Meadow Lake. Ate vending machine peanut butter crackers in the FBO for two hours and watched it rain on my plans. Zulu is not a suggestion. Zulu is six hours from my watch. In the winter it's seven, which I will also forget.

Jordan read it out loud. Claire laughed before she got to the crackers, and then put the dish towel over her face for a second, and when she took it down she said, He called me from the vending machine. I remember. He said he was being responsible and he wanted credit for it. She looked over at Jordan. Abby texted me. I didn't know Abby had my number. It just said, she turned around early and didn't argue. That's the whole text.
Is Daddy's writing in there about clouds? Ellie said, without turning around from the window.
About a storm. He got stuck somewhere and had to wait it out.
Jordan looked down at the page. The handwriting got bigger in the part about the black wall. Some. Then he landed and ate crackers out of a machine for two hours. Which was the smart part.

Ellie chewed on that. Out over the Divide the rain was dragging itself back south, the dark flat base lifting off the hilltops like a lid coming off a pot, and way behind it there was a strip of that hard rinsed blue you only get afterward. Is the flat part the shelf?
Same shelf, Jordan said. Somebody just piled way too much on it.
Claire's hand went to the back of Ellie's chair. Then, after a second, to Jordan's shoulder, and it stayed there while the thunder grumbled off toward Kansas and the gutters ran.
